title: DR Pixel: Page-Native Deep Research with Vision-Language Models
authors: Tiansheng Hu, Yichuan Wang, James V. Talwar et al.
abstract: Complex documents such as scientific papers contain rich information in tables, figures, and equations; however, existing deep research (DR) agents typically reduce papers to OCR-extracted text. We instead ask whether vision-language models (VLMs) can enable page-native deep research: directly retrieving and reasoning over rendered document page images. title: Bridging Low-Level Image Fusion and High-Level Semantic Understanding
authors: Guangyuan Dong, Lingdong Shen, Xudong Zhang et al.
abstract: Remote sensing image fusion and semantic interpretation are usually optimized separately, so reconstruction quality need not preserve downstream retrieval utility. We propose LANCE, which uses structured language as an explicit, indexable semantic state. A frozen vision-language model maps the input to a closed-vocabulary text record; a language-conditioned generator fuses the imagery; and a dense verifier with a differentiable continuous summarizer re-describes the output. Text-text consistency

title: PGuard: A Native, Streaming, and Plug-in Guardrail for Multimodal Large Language Models
authors: Junyu Lin, Mengjie Wu, Yonghao Dong et al.
abstract: As streaming generation becomes the dominant serving paradigm for both text-only and multimodal large language models, ensuring safety throughout the generation process has become a critical challenge. We introduce PGuard, a native, streaming, and plug-in guardrail that transforms safety monitoring from an external serving dependency into an integrated capability of the backbone model. PGuard directly leverages the backbone's intermediate representations for token-level safety detection, without

title: As Expected? Efficient LLM Planning via Expectation-Observation Consistency Verification
authors: Qingfu Zhu, Huanyang Zheng, Ting Liu et al.
abstract: LLM planning often relies on reactive executors (e.g., ReAct) that generate a single action at each step to remain grounded in the latest observations, incurring substantial inference cost. Batched executors reduce this cost by predicting multiple actions in a single model invocation, yet they are prone to compounding errors, as intermediate observations are ignored. title: Exploiting Textual Semantics for Robust Cross-View Object Correspondence
authors: Bing Fan, Yunhe Feng, Yan Huang et al.
abstract: Cross-view object correspondence (CVOC) aims to establish associations of the same target between query and search videos captured from different viewpoints. Existing methods often rely on visual cues for CVOC. Despite recent progress, these methods struggle in complicated scenarios with substantial viewpoint changes and appearance variations, due to lacking sufficient target information. title: TrafficInstruct: A Multi-Task Network Traffic Dataset and Benchmark for Instruction Tuning
authors: Zhengdao Li, Hui Wen, Zixuan Wan et al.
abstract: Instruction tuning for multi-task network traffic analysis requires data with clearly defined sources, supervision targets, and evaluation conditions. We introduce TrafficInstruct, a newly collected dataset comprising raw packet captures and 55,000 structured supervised fine-tuning records across ten tasks: malware traffic detection, botnet detection, malicious DNS-over-HTTPS detection, Web attack detection, advanced persistent threat detection, encrypted VPN detection, Tor behavior detection, e

title: Specificity Bias and the Wikipedia Paradox: An xAI Analysis of AI Text Detectors under Domain Shift
authors: Nico Morloher, Johannes Reschke, Mohamed Mady
abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) demands reliable detection of human-authored versus synthetic text. However, current Transformer-based detectors often experience severe performance degradation during domain shifts and operate as opaque classifiers. This paper investigates the robustness and interpretability of fine-tuned Transformer models (DistilBERT, RoBERTa) by evaluating them against a custom out-of-distribution (OOD) dataset of hyper-local news synthesized via open-s

title: DINOFAS: Bonafide-Centric Representation Learning for Face Anti-Spoofing
authors: Shakeel Muhammad Ibrahim, Muhammad Sohail Ibrahim, Muhammad Shahid Jabbar et al.
abstract: Face anti-spoofing (FAS) models often learn attack- and dataset-specific cues that degrade performance under unseen acquisition conditions and presentation attacks. We present DINOFAS, a DINOv3-based framework that formulates FAS as bonafide-centric representation learning. title: Train the Sampler You Run: Few-Step Masked Diffusion Language Models via Mixture-Likelihood Fine-Tuning
authors: Amin Najafgholizadeh
abstract: When a masked diffusion language model is sampled in a few parallel steps in a random order, the model actually run is a mixture over reveal plans, while cross-entropy training fits token conditionals rather than this mixture. We introduce mixture-likelihood fine-tuning (Mix-FT), which fine-tunes a pretrained model on an importance-weighted bound of its own sampler's likelihood, with no teacher and no change to the architecture or the sampler. title: PixelBench: Can LLMs Understand and Generate Images Pixel by Pixel?
authors: Haoquan Zhang, Feiyang Liu, Juanxi Tian et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate visual assets through text-based formats such as SVG and CAD, but these symbolic representations describe images using high-level primitives rather than explicit raster values. We ask whether LLMs can instead generate pixel images directly through their existing vocabulary, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. title: Spatial Transfusion: From Structured Spatial Scene Understanding to Generation and Editing
authors: Jaeyeon Kim, Sebastian Braun, Hannes Gamper
abstract: Spatial audio conveys not only what sounds are present, but where they originate and how they interact with the environment. Recent audio-language models increasingly understand and reason about such scenes, yet spatial audio understanding, generation, and editing remain largely separate. We present Spatial Transfusion, a unified first-order ambisonics (FOA) framework that extends a pretrained spatial audio understanding model to generation and editing through flow matching over VAE latents. We

title: Written Once, Read Differently How Language Models Own Answers Steer Their Next Ones
authors: Marcus Armstrong
abstract: When a language model answers a yes/no question, that answer changes how it answers a different question about the same entity. We study this \emph{self-commitment} in 22 open-weight models from four families (0.5B--72B parameters), fixing the model's first answer and measuring the shift in its second across 3,600 question pairs about 120 entities. title: DepthGraft: Structural Regularization through Hierarchical Cross-Layer KV Reconstruction
authors: Xiaohan Qin, Xiangdong Zhang, Yu Wang et al.
abstract: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. title: A Fine-Grained Hierarchy and Benchmark for State Tracking in Language Models
authors: Jackson Petty, William Merrill, Ashish Sabharwal
abstract: Theoretical limitations of transformers on state tracking---the ability to track information about entities or variables over long contexts---have motivated new recurrent language modeling (LM) architectures such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN). These architectures have, in particular, been benchmarked against the $S_5$ word problem, a theoretically hard state-tracking task that captures abilities such as code evaluation under arbitrary variable assignment. title: Towards Multi-Value Alignment via Value Localization in LLMs
authors: Xueqi Ma, Yanbei Jiang, Xingjun Ma et al.
abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with multiple, potentially conflicting human values remains challenging, as existing multi-objective alignment methods often require costly fine-tuning and provide limited insight into the internal mechanisms underlying value-related behaviors. In this work, we investigate multi-value alignment from a mechanistic interpretability perspective by identifying value-sensitive attention heads (value heads) in LLMs. Using a probing-based value localization framewo

title: Which Words a Model Fears: From a Refusal Direction to a Vocabulary-Wide Fear Lexicon
authors: Boyuan Zhang, Mohammad Zandsalimy, Shanu Sushmita
abstract: Whether an aligned language model refuses depends in part on which words a prompt contains, regardless of whether those words carry the request's meaning. Harm words shift the hidden state at the generation boundary along a component shared across prompts and words, which crossed differencing extracts as a single direction. title: Evaluating Uncertainty Calibration in Probabilistic Time Series Foundation Models
authors: Thomas Decker, Volker Tresp
abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are increasingly used for probabilistic forecasting across diverse domains, yet the reliability of their uncertainty estimates remains poorly understood. In this work, we study uncertainty calibration in probabilistic TSFMs from a broader methodological and empirical perspective. We introduce a taxonomy of how TSFMs represent predictive uncertainty and develop a fine-grained evaluation framework for calibration in multi-horizon forecasting that distinguishes

title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified
authors: Yuqi Jia, Yunjie Tian, Jiayu Zheng et al.
abstract: We introduce Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model that combines strong and broad agentic capabilities with a remarkably simple training recipe. Axion 1.0 is trained in only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). title: Can Coding Agents Sustain Continual Evolution without Forgetting?
authors: Shangziqi Zhao, Yitong Zhang, Jia Li
abstract: Recently, harness self-evolution has emerged as an important paradigm for improving agent performance. Prior studies show that evolving the agent harness can effectively enhance agent capabilities without modifying the foundation model's parameters. We find that existing approaches largely study agent evolution on a single task. In practice, coding agents may need to handle multiple task types over time. Whether an agent harness can continuously evolve across multiple tasks without suffering fro

title: LaBraM at Scale: Scaling Data and Models for EEG Pretraining
authors: Jun-Yu Pan, Ruicheng Yin, Bao-Liang Lu et al.
abstract: LaBraM, an early EEG foundation model, demonstrated that large-scale EEG pretraining can yield strong representations for diverse downstream tasks. Building on this foundation, we expand pretraining data and model capacity while retaining its core encoder and objective. We train ten encoders with 5.8 million to 1.97 billion parameters on three EEG collections spanning 25,067 to 79,910 hours, adapting signal preparation and training to heterogeneous recordings. Across 23 tasks, Atom-L* reaches 59

title: Preprocessing Choices in Fine-Tuning Data Matter: Utility and Demographic Sensitivity in LLM-Based Recommendation
authors: Furkan Yasir Goksu, Yaren Yilmaz, Sule Gunduz Oguducu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have introduced a generative approach to recommendation, producing item lists from textual representations of user histories and item information. However, this generative setting raises challenges concerning output validity, prompt consistency, and sensitivity to demographic descriptors. In this work, we investigate how preprocessing choices in fine-tuning data affect recommendation utility and fairness-related behavior in a generative LLM-based recommender system.

title: PACERec: Progressive Adaptation of LLM Item Embeddings with Collaborative Evidence for Recommendation
authors: Junzhao Huang, Xi Wu, Zihan Wang et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) embeddings have been increasingly adopted in sequential recommendation to encode static item attributes and alleviate the limitations of item ID embeddings under sparse interactions. title: Specification-Aware Predictive Uncertainty Decomposition
authors: Roman Vashurin, Mikhail Seleznyov, Assel Yermekova et al.
abstract: Classical decompositions of predictive uncertainty, such as the information-theoretic one, are defined for a fixed representation $x$ of the input object. They do not consider that $x$ may be incomplete, nor do they measure how much the missing information can affect the prediction. In Large Language Models, users can clarify an underspecified input without any retraining. title: PlagiaCorpus: A Bilingual, Adversarial, and Cross-Lingual Dataset for Forensic Plagiarism Detection
authors: Adel Ammar, Serry Sibaee, Wadii Boulila
abstract: PlagiaCorpus is a bilingual Arabic-English dataset for benchmarking plagiarism and text-reuse detection, including reuse produced by large language models (LLMs) and reuse across languages. It contains 198,643 text records: a source corpus of 34,885 passages drawn from English and Arabic Wikipedia and two openly licensed book collections, and 163,758 queries (147,381 for training and 16,377 for testing). title: Why Tabular Foundation Models Excel on Relational Data They Have Never Seen
authors: Linjie Xu, Yiqun Hu, Jixiang He et al.
abstract: Given a relational database (RDB) storing heterogeneous tabular information, how can we predict missing (or future) values in some target column of interest? As candidate targets are numerous in enterprise settings, it is preferable to avoid learning a new model from scratch each time there is a new prediction task. Frozen foundation models (FMs) based on in-context learning (ICL) and RDB-specific pre-training provide a viable solution, but the ideal design still remains largely unresolved. Perh

title: What makes a theorem interesting? Operationalizing interestingness for open-ended exploration
authors: Silvère Gangloff
abstract: An agent that explores, whether it generates conjectures or research ideas, must decide which of them are worth keeping. This judgment of interestingness is usually delegated to a hand-picked proxy or to a language model, neither of which is known to correspond to what humans actually value. I study it for mathematical theorems, by observing which results mathematicians single out in formal libraries and in papers. I model each way of singling out results as an evaluator that weights features of

title: Tug of Watts: A study on the Energy - Accuracy Trade-off of Large Language Models on Medical Question Answering Tasks
authors: Viju Sudhi, Giulio Billi, Andreea Scrob et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in medical question answering (QA) systems. While recent works aim at incrementally improving the downstream task accuracy, an empirical estimation of the models' energy consumption and the associated carbon footprints is often overlooked. In this study, we demonstrate how practitioners can estimate energy consumption and arrive at reliable emission estimates for medical QA tasks available in the OpenMedical-LLM leaderboard by investigating 13 L

title: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding
authors: Tianyu Liu, Jun Zhang, Wenjie Huang et al.
abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by reducing the sequential cost of token-by-token generation. Advanced SD methods reduce proposal cost with parallel drafters that predict entire blocks in one forward pass, but overall speedup still depends on acceptance length. On-policy distillation (OPD) can push well-trained drafters beyond acceptance-length plateaus, yet conventional pipelines collect supervision through sequential draft-and-verify rollouts. title: Creating Hybrid Interactive Narrative Systems with LLM: From Formal Description to Evaluation
authors: Jules Clerc, Domitile Lourdeaux, Mohamed Sallak et al.
abstract: Interactive narratives let users shape a story while an Experience Manager (EM) keeps it coherent, balancing player freedom against authorial control. Large Language Models now enable a new generation of hybrid EMs, which combine run-time generation from free-text input with symbolic narrative control. title: Rethinking Neural Decompilation: Candidate Selection as the Hidden Bottleneck
authors: Felix Mächtle, Gautham Sriram, Manjil Neupane et al.
abstract: Reverse engineering obfuscated binaries is a core task in malware analysis and software security auditing. While neural decompilers based on Large Language Models (LLMs) have improved the readability and functional fidelity of recovered code over heuristic tools such as Ghidra and IDA Pro, a substantial gap remains between best-sample performance and practical single-output accuracy, particularly under code obfuscation. title: Is your LLM an Agressive Narcissist with Depression? Analyzing Psychological Portraits of Large Language Models
authors: Polina Fedorinina, Anna Fattakhova, Nadezhda Romanova et al.
abstract: Nowadays, interaction with AI requires caution not only regarding the factual reliability of generated content but also regarding personality markers that models may implicitly transmit during dialogue that can subtly influence users' perception of information. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale experimental study in which 22 large language models complete 11 psychological inventories. title: Investigating the effects of the patch size in Time Series Foundation Models
authors: Jad Yehya, Andrei-Tiberiu Pantea, Aymeric Dieuleveut et al.
abstract: Patch size is a central design choice in patch-based time-series foundation models, controlling temporal resolution, sequence length, and computational cost. We study how this choice interacts with transformer architecture through a controlled comparison of encoder-only and decoder-only forecasting models trained with the same data mixture and optimization budget. title: Human-Supervised Artificial Intelligence Researchers in Electric Power Systems: Knowledge, Physics, Simulation, and Governance for Large Language Models
authors: Xiangrui Meng, Jingcheng Liu, Ke Wang et al.
abstract: Conclusions in power-system research require a clear evidential basis. Researchers need to understand the data sources, modelling assumptions, and solution procedures to assess the conditions under which a conclusion holds. Large language models (LLMs) can help researchers extract information from documents and translate research requests into code and tool calls, but their outputs still require physical validation. title: LLMs Cannot Be Neutral: Gender Sensitivity Across Candidates, Evaluators, and Models
authors: Danial Amin, Joni Salminen, Bernard J. Jansen
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate candidates for professional roles, raising concerns about their sensitivity to demographic identities. We examine how candidate and evaluator gender assignments affect decisions by LLM-as-a-Judge (LaJ) models and decision language models (DLMs). title: HistoTx: Early fusion of H&E images and spatial transcriptomics at varying spatial transcriptomics resolution with self-supervised learning
authors: Alice Driessen, Emil Malmsten, Steffen Wolf et al.
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression across tissue sections and, when integrated with whole slide images, jointly captures both morphological architecture and molecular activity to provide a rich, multimodal view of tissue biology. ML approaches combining spatial transcriptomics and WSIs typically learn a mapping from morphological features to molecular profiles via contrastive alignment or supervised fine-tuning of pathology foundation models. title: SearchInject: Retrieval Exposure Control for Indirect Prompt Injection in Language-Model Search
authors: Kainan Zhou, Gangzhen Qian, Janet Sung et al.
abstract: An indirect prompt injection can affect a search-augmented large language model only after its carrier page reaches model context. SearchInject controls this admission decision with a joint score combining retrieval relevance, search-abuse cues, instruction likelihood, and two relevance interactions. title: From Language to Country to Valence: A Multilingual Audit of Stereotype Bias Across LLMs
authors: Zihao Sun
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for education, recruitment, workplace decision support, and other consequential applications, making pre-deployment social-bias detection essential. Yet major benchmarks are English-centred or translated, focus mainly on negative stereotypes, and may miss linguistic and cultural variation. title: BasisKV: Value Latents for Communication and Key Routing
authors: Lixun Zhang, Zishan Shao, Kangning Cui et al.
abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is increasingly constrained by the cost of maintaining an ever-growing KV-cache. Low-rank K/V projections provide a promising way to compress the KV-cache with minimal quality loss, but prior work has largely optimized KV-cache compression in isolation, leaving distributed inference, especially with tensor parallelism where attention computation is partitioned across multiple GPUs, largely underexplored. title: Latent Spectral Prompting for Multimodal Hyperspectral Object Tracking
authors: Wangshu Cai, Jun Zhou, Lei Wang et al.
abstract: Hyperspectral videos provide rich spectral signatures for robust tracking under challenging conditions such as camouflage and low illumination. However, limited hyperspectral annotations and the large RGB-hyperspectral domain gap hinder the direct use of modern temporally pretrained RGB trackers. We propose SProTrack, a multimodal framework that transfers temporal knowledge from pretrained RGB trackers to the hyperspectral domain through latent spectral prompting. title: Same Sentence, Different Construct: Identity-Swapped Rationales Reveal Measurement Non-Invariance in LLM Hate Speech Classifiers
authors: Wenchang Wang, Yue Song
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as measurement instruments for socially consequential constructs such as hate speech, and are typically validated by their aggregate agreement with human labels. A valid instrument must also apply the same construct to every group it measures. We test this requirement using 421 \hc{} templates that are instantiated identically for seven protected groups, so that only the identity term varies. title: Does a Norwegian further-trained model give more outdated legal values than its base model? A preregistered paired comparison of Borealis 2 and Gemma 4
authors: Eirik Botten Nicolaysen
abstract: We compare how often two released language models give outdated numeric values from Norwegian statutes and regulations: NbAiLab/borealis2-26b-a4b-preview (Borealis 2), which the National Library of Norway further trained from google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it (Gemma 4), and Gemma 4 itself. title: D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment Enables VLMs as Zero-Shot Robotic Reward Models
authors: Marius Memmel, Shawn Yin, Urvi Rutia et al.
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold promise for zero-shot video task-progress estimation in robot learning, yet existing frameworks frequently suffer from confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed executions due to implicit success assumptions or relative temporal ranking designs. Naive prompting of frontier models collapses into a binary success detector that fails to capture nuanced, non-linear progress and failures. title: CISA: Retrofitting Dense Attention Models with Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention
authors: Mohammed Dabbah, Izhak Golan, Oren Tropp et al.
abstract: Long-context LLM inference is costly because attention repeatedly reads a growing key-value (KV) history. We introduce Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention (CISA), which retrofits pretrained dense attention models without gradient updates. CISA selects fixed-size KV chunks using compact summaries of existing keys, avoiding token-level indexing and a separate full-length index cache. title: Tune the Baseline First: Most of Muon's Scaled Weight Decay Gain Is a Tuning Gap, but Its Small Real Advantage Grows With Model Size
authors: Esther Xin
abstract: Scaled weight decay for Muon (Muon-SW) has been reported to train language models more efficiently than constant decoupled weight decay, but such comparisons usually reuse one learning-rate (LR) and weight-decay (WD) setting for both methods. We re-run the comparison under the MAI-Base-2 protocol: LR and WD are tuned jointly through their product for each method, on a source-scaled mixture-of-experts (MoE) scaling ladder (1.9M to 15M active parameters) that holds tokens per active parameter and

title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
authors: Kunjun Li, Wenhao Chai, Yihao Liang et al.
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates memory-bound LLM decoding with a lightweight drafter, and parallel drafters extend this speedup by drafting a whole block in one forward pass. However, it remains unclear whether their released systems (stock) attain the full speedup that parallel drafting permits. We identify three challenges. title: RecRSI: Mechanism-Guided Discovery of Recommendation Algorithms
authors: Tingran Gan, Zhouziyue Lu, Dian Jin et al.
abstract: Improving recommendation algorithms for the Web requires coordinating interacting design choices and learning from experiments. We present RecRSI, an LLM-based research framework that uses mechanism hypotheses to organize algorithm discovery. Each hypothesis links a proposed mechanism change to a reference design, a rationale, and an expected observation. title: RecGroupMemory: Feedback-Aware Cohort Memory for E-Commerce Recommendation
authors: Wendong Zhang, Weipeng Huang, Zhixin Ma et al.
abstract: Cohort memory can support LLM-based recommendation planning through group-level user profiles and advice. As outcome feedback becomes available, this guidance may need to be updated while preserving the underlying observations. We present RecGroupMemory, a workflow that provides this memory to an orchestration LLM and separates memory construction from feedback-based revision. title: SGR-OPSD: Learning from Subgoal Plans with Graph-Regularized Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Shu Liu, Yang Chong, WenShi Chen et al.
abstract: OPSD provides dense supervision for agentic reinforcement learning through privileged information feedback. However, existing privileged information often lacks explicit task-progression planning, while teacher-student log-probability gaps reflect shifts in model preference rather than true task progress. title: Attribution-based diagnostics for single-cell foundation models
authors: Farnoush Rezaei Jafari, Tristan Lazard, Kenza Bouzid et al.
affiliations: BIFOLD - Berlin Institute for the Foundations of Learning and Data
abstract: Single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for in-silico biological discovery, yet predictive performance alone does not reveal whether their decisions rely on biologically meaningful signals or model-specific shortcuts. We systematically investigate post-hoc attribution of downstream predictions across two tasks: cell-type annotation using pretrained Cell2Sentence and scGPT models, and perturbation prediction using scGPT+STATE in a controlled setting. title: Enhancing Stock Market Information Retrieval with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Huan Phong Thai, Thu Anh Ngoc Le, Nhu Huynh Thi Le et al.
abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has been widely applied in financial domains, enabling automated analysis and retrieval of stock market information. However, traditional NLP-based systems often struggle with maintaining contextual accuracy and generating relevant responses in dynamic financial environments. title: WASP-Mem: Let Agent Organize Procedural Memory. Human Spend Effort on Diagnosis
authors: Peizhi Niu, Ge Shi, Vaibhav Gorde et al.
abstract: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. title: Measure Before You Repair: An Explainable Agent for Blind Restoration of Multi-Artifact 3-D MRI
authors: Necati Sefercioglu, Mehmet Ozan Unal, Metin Ertas et al.
abstract: A brain MRI scan can carry an unknown mix of artifacts, so restoration has to be blind, yet most deep-learning methods are built to correct one known artifact. We present Dx-Rx, an agent in which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) measures suspected artifacts before it repairs them. To our knowledge, it is the first agent to restore whole 3-D MRI volumes, whereas earlier MRI agents restore 2-D slices. title: SLATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Long-Horizon API Selection in E-commerce Tool Use
authors: Rongzhe Wei, Ge Shi, Min Cheng et al.
abstract: Enterprises increasingly want LLM agents to automate standard operating procedures over their software stacks -- mapping each step of a procedure to the right call among thousands of internal APIs, without hand-authored step-to-API mappings. The core difficulty is API selection at scale: choosing and composing the correct tools over a long horizon, judged only by whether the overall task succeeds. title: Measuring Model-Specific Alignment Drift in LLM-Based Opinion Dynamics
authors: Nataša Djurdjevac Conrad, Sebastian Pokutta, Christof Schütte
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as synthetic participants in opinion-dynamics experiments, often assuming that an agent's behaviour is fully determined by its prompt. We test this assumption with a framework in which LLM agents discuss a contested policy issue over repeated rounds while their stance is quantified by a fixed psychometric instrument independent of any dynamics model. title: ProofPaths: An AI Agent Framework for Assessing Student Reasoning
authors: Mohsen Hariri, Vipin Chaudhary
abstract: Students can use large language models to complete assignments, but a correct solution does not establish whether they understand the reasoning behind it. Individualized interviews can probe that understanding but require recurring staff effort. We introduce ProofPaths, an AI agentic framework that combines rubric-based grading with individualized and interactive interviews. title: Performance, Scalability and Maintenance: An Experimental Study of RPA vs. Autonomous Agents in the Healthcare Domain
authors: Daniel Schulz, Pedro Cabral Buchaim, Bernardo Soares et al.
abstract: Healthcare information systems are fragmented, and retrieving data from legacy web portals is a recurrent need. Robotic Process Automation (RPA) is deterministic but sensitive to interface changes, whereas autonomous agents based on large language models (Agent Process Automation, APA) promise adaptability at a higher computational cost. Following Design Science Research, we developed and compared an RPA solution (Playwright) and an APA solution (browser-use, LangGraph and Gemini 2.5 Flash-lite)

title: El Agente Fármaco: A Scalable AI Scientist for Drug Discovery
authors: Marcel Müller, Mohammad Ghazi Vakili, Yoshihiro Ogura et al.
abstract: Computational drug discovery offers a growing range of tools for proposing and evaluating molecules, but combining them and deciding what to do next still requires substantial expert effort. Here, we introduce El Agente Fármaco, an AI scientist that uses modern large language model (LLM) technology to turn discovery goals expressed in everyday language into complex, scalable computational screening workflows. The agentic harness selects scientific tools, reviews their results, and adjusts subseq

title: The Web Doesn't Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents
authors: Geyuan Wang, Shunyu Liu, Siyuan Liang et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for empowering search agents to tackle complex information-seeking tasks. However, since acquiring external information necessitates web search, these agents are highly susceptible to various adversarial attacks (e.g., malicious information injection or stealthy context manipulation). Existing attack strategies inevitably rely on static and human-crafted templates, failing to emulate the dynamic and complex nature of real-world threats. In this pap

title: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents
authors: Zhishang Xiang, Yunbo Tang, Zhongqiao Liu et al.
abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit

title: ScienceVision: Can AI Observe and Reason Like a Scientist?
authors: Tianyi Ma, Jing Gu, Haozhe Zhao et al.
abstract: Scientific discovery builds on accurate observations interpreted through domain knowledge and reasoning. For scientific 3D data, this requires understanding structures and spatial relationships, from protein contacts to anatomical organization. Existing multimodal benchmarks largely evaluate text and 2D images, while scientific 3D evaluations vary in representations and protocols across disciplines, limiting cross-disciplinary comparison. To assess these foundational capabilities, we introduce S

title: CAREFUL-Bench: Effect-Aware, Judge-Free Evaluation of Multi-Turn LLM Function Calling
authors: Alexander Kovalenko, Artem Redchych
abstract: The multi-turn checker of the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) checks only the final state of a simulated service, never the calls that produced it. Extra calls cost nothing, no function doc says what a function does, and the scripted user never answers a proposal, so a model that asks before deleting or paying fails the turn; 322 of the 734 reference turns in the base category act destructively without confirmation. We add effect information to BFCL without replacing it. Effect decl

title: On the Primacy Bias in RLVR Training
authors: Phuc Minh Nguyen, Ngoc-Hieu Nguyen, Parshin Shojaee et al.
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models. However, it still remains unclear whether RLVR can extend reasoning capabilities beyond what is already encoded in the base model. In this paper, we study this question through the lens of primacy bias: the tendency of models to over-rely on already-learned representations, disproportionately improving performance on problems they already han

title: Exploit or conform? How norm utility prompting changes the way LLMs use community beliefs
authors: Leon Klingborg, Theodor Cimpeanu, Alexander J. Stewart
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) serve both as tools for aiding human decision-making in everyday life and as models of human agents in experimental simulation studies. Alignment on prototypical social decisions -- such as whether to cooperate on a collective action -- therefore has immediate practical consequences for researchers and for society at large. Here we systematically explore the impact of ``norm utility'' -- the non-material components of utility that account for an individual's desire t

title: Whose startup does the AI back? An algorithm audit of reputation and demographic signals in LLM-assisted crowdfunding
authors: Mirza Samad Ahmed Baig, Syeda Anshrah Gillani
abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly advise backers on which crowdfunding campaigns to support. LLMs have known race and gender problems, and it is unsettled whether they reproduce, erase, or reverse the discrimination documented in entrepreneurial finance. We ask when, and through which decision process, LLM assistants use founders' gender and ethnicity. In a pre-specified choice-based conjoint experiment, seven LLMs chose among five synthetic campaigns with independently randomiz

title: Balancing Chain-of-Thought and Answer Supervision for Small Language Models on Medical Question Answering
authors: Le Zhou, Xiao Luo, Chinmay Chandra et al.
abstract: Small language models (<=9B parameters) can support local medical question answering (QA) while reducing privacy and latency concerns, but effective fine-tuning remains challenging. This paper compares two chain-of-thought (CoT) supervised fine-tuning methods: Uniform-across-Sequence (UaS), which applies equal loss weighting to the full CoT-and-answer sequence, and Segment-weighted (SwS), which separately weights CoT and answer losses. We evaluate six general- and medical-domain models on mul

title: PianoBench: Evaluating Musical Perception and Reasoning in Language Models
authors: Louis Bradshaw, Irmak Bukey, Daniel Chenyu Lin et al.
abstract: Multimodal language models continue to improve on broad music understanding benchmarks, but which musical features can they perceive and reason about? We investigate this question by introducing PianoBench, a benchmark that tasks language models with reasoning about musical performances across congruent acoustic and symbolic input representations. PianoBench is derived from our new multimodal, training-scale dataset comprising more than 20,000 hours of interleaved transcripts of music and spoken

title: Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging for Efficient Long-to-Short Reasoning
authors: Zeqiu Yu, Xuesheng Zhang, Wenxiao Zhao et al.
abstract: Long-to-Short (L2S) model merging seeks to combine the strong reasoning capability of long chain-of-thought models with the concise style of base models, but existing methods that rely on linear interpolation and first-order activation statistics fail to capture how the loss landscape responds to parameter displacement, leading to degraded accuracy on hard tasks. We propose Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging (LHM), a training-free framework that replaces heuristic statistics with lightweight second-o

title: EpiLoRA: Fusing Many LoRA Adapters into Low-Precision GEMMs for Serving and RL
authors: Hieu Tran, Hong Yu
abstract: Low-rank adapters (LoRA) let one base model serve many fine-tuned variants: multi-tenant engines keep a single copy of the base and batch the requests of many tenants, each with its own adapter. As base models move to 8-bit (FP8) and 4-bit formats, their general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) become cheaper, but the adapters do not: engines run them as separate small GPU kernels beside the GEMM, whose latency takes a growing share of every decoding step. title: LoRA-Patch: Defending Against Backdoored LoRA Adapters via Directional Steering
authors: Shengyan Huo, Peihai Jiang, Xixiang Lyu et al.
abstract: Third-party LoRA adapters introduce serious backdoor risks: malicious adapters can maintain normal task performance while embedding hidden, trigger-activated behaviors, making them difficult to detect through standard utility evaluations. Existing removal-based defenses typically sanitize backdoored models by updating, pruning, distilling, or mixing model parameters. However, these approaches are misaligned with adapter-based deployment, where the trusted base model is expected to remain frozen.

title: Language Model Augmented Decision Transformer for Multi-Task Offline Reinforcement Learning
authors: Xinbo Zhao, Yuhang Liu, Xin Zhang et al.
abstract: Offline multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) aims to learn a unified policy from heterogeneous offline datasets that generalizes across tasks. However, existing offline MTRL methods often struggle with two fundamental issues: severe per-task data scarcity and limited cross-task generalization. title: Replay for LLM Continual Learning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
authors: Yiqiao Qiu
abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) distills several domain experts into one student and is used in the post-training of recent large language models. It trains on all domains at once, so every expert must be available at the same time. In practice, capabilities often arrive one after another, and the experts of earlier domains may be gone when a new domain is learned. title: Reasoning is topologically simple
authors: Chris Kapulkin, Nathan Kershaw
abstract: We formulate and investigate the hypothesis that reasoning text has simpler co-occurrence topology than non-reasoning text, and that higher-quality reasoning has simpler co-occurrence topology than lower-quality reasoning. We discuss and test applications to AI safety and AI evaluation.

title: Query-based Submodular Data Selection for Efficient Instruction Tuning
authors: Zhenghao Zhao, Yasutomo Kawanishi, Huihuo Zheng et al.
abstract: As large language models are fine-tuned for increasingly specialized tasks, their performance depends more on which training examples are selected than on how many. Given a large heterogeneous training pool and a small target set specifying the desired capability, targeted data selection aims to find a compact subset that maximizes downstream performance. Existing methods score each candidate independently against the target and select the top-ranked examples, yet this point-wise strategy ignore

title: Recursa: Toward Recursively Self-Improving Foundation Model Systems
authors: Erkang Zhu, Yin Lin, Xiaorong Shi et al.
abstract: Foundation models in changing environments can encounter unfamiliar domain knowledge that their original training did not cover. However, new domains rarely provide large amounts of expert-created training data or reliable supervisory signals for further training. We introduce Recursa, a foundation model system that adapts to new domains by learning from its own experience without human experts or a stronger teacher model. Recursa uses a knowledge repository to store what it learns: domain-speci

title: Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the Market
authors: Amir Dehkordi, Alireza Kargarzadeh, Nariman Khaledian et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) read company news at scale, and backtests suggest that their readings predict stock returns. We ask how much of that predictability survives a test that rules out look-ahead, memorization and selection. We propose OLIVIA, a protocol for such tests: point-in-time inputs with company identities masked, selection on validation data only, an analysis plan frozen by cryptographic hash, and a test period unblinded once through a logged lock. We apply it to AI decision mode

title: A Conditional Mutual Information Analysis of Response Variety in Language Models
authors: R. I. Cukier
abstract: Large language models provide a variety of responses at inference (generation) that conventionally depend on a temperature parameter. Using a conditional mutual information approach, a quantitative, entropy based analysis of response variety is given. Three limiting behaviors are defined: arbiter, independent (conditionally) and neutral (deterministic) that span no to maximal mutual information. We give examples of each behavior and suggest their application to: temperature analysis, language an

title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
authors: Serdarcan Dilbaz, Arjun Krishna, Kiran Kamble et al.
abstract: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. title: AlgoPilot: Cross-Paradigm Reasoning in Language Models via Strategy Selection and Guidance
authors: Yilun Hao, Ruixiao Yang, Hudson Hilal et al.
abstract: Real-world problems span diverse domains, including program synthesis, symbolic reasoning, planning, and optimization, and often require fundamentally different solution paradigms. A central challenge for LLM-based reasoning is twofold: identifying an appropriate problem-solving approach and formulating it correctly. In this paper, we propose AlgoPilot, a cross-paradigm reasoning framework that enables adaptive selection of the solving approaches and structured problem formulation prior to execu

title: EvoGroup: A Self-Evolving Harness for Group Agents in Shared Contexts
authors: Xinyi Xu, Xiaoyang Li, Yucheng Feng et al.
abstract: With the rise of Group Agent such as Claude Tag, agents increasingly serve as digital workers for long-term team collaboration. These agents operate over shared contexts that continuously accumulate through multi-user interactions. However, existing agent memory systems are mainly designed for individual users and struggle to capture group-level knowledge in shared contexts, including group relationships and collaboratively formed knowledge. Manual memory strategies further limit adaptation to d

title: LLM-based NPCs in Video Games: A Systematic Mapping Study
authors: Dilan Mian, Jeremy Bradbury, Yann-Gaël Guéhéneuc et al.
abstract: For decades, non-player characters (NPCs) have been driven by rule-based systems whose personalities and interactions are scripted before release. Large language models (LLMs) promise NPCs that converse openly, adapt to new situations, and behave in ways developers did not fully author, prompting a wave of research and commercial experimentation. Yet the field lacks a unified picture of what has been built, how well it works, and at what cost. We address this gap with a systematic mapping study

title: Toward Agentic AI-Ready Workflows in Built Environment Organizations: Knowledge Structures and Interoperability Challenges
authors: Ahmet Bahaddin Ersoz, Justin McHenry, Yevgeniya Kovalchuk et al.
abstract: The rise of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) in the built environment is shifting attention from isolated AI tools toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act across project and organizational workflows. The effectiveness of such systems depends not only on large language model capabilities, but also on the readiness of heterogeneous data environments across the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector. These environments combine structured sources, such as CAD and B

title: RAG-TRACE: Tracing Measurement Evidence and Diagnostic Completeness in AI-Generated ECG Reports
authors: Elyas Irankhah, Shahed Salehzehi, Parisa Hosseini
abstract: Purpose: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can introduce electrocardiogram (ECG) criteria that lack patient-specific measurement support. This study evaluates the reliability of retrieved diagnostic criteria in AI-generated ECG reports. Methods: We analyzed 1,083 human-validated PTB-XL patient records using a library of 47 criteria cards, including 33 without numeric verification rules. Language models generated structured reports with and without retrieval. Criterion applicability was evalua

title: Qubrio: High-Performance Quantum Compilation via Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration
authors: Jixuan Ruan, Zhuo Cui, Zhengding Hu et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer an adaptable alternative to traditional quantum compilation heuristics, which bottleneck progress by demanding costly manual redesigns whenever hardware evolves. However, naive single-pass LLM approaches fail under the unique challenges introduced by quantum compilation. We introduce Qubrio, a practical agentic framework that significantly reduces heuristic redesigns through a three-level decomposition. By (1) partitioning programs into sequential operation sta

title: Multi-Agent Collusion and the J-Space
authors: Marco Molinari, Gabriele Bettineschi
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), and they introduce the risk of coordination among agents that might escape human oversight. The J-space has been used to uncover deception in single LLMs, but its use for uncovering and steering collusion between agents remains unexplored. title: ParetoSaddler: Pareto-Guided Optimization of Agent Harnesses for Quality and Cost
authors: Xingzhi Qian, Sungho Park, Rongyuan Tan et al.
abstract: Harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents without modifying model weights, but existing methods primarily optimize response quality. Extending them to joint quality--cost optimization introduces a challenge: applying the deployment preference during intermediate updates can prematurely reject candidates that are valuable for later improvements. We introduce ParetoSaddler, which addresses this mismatch by separating intermediate candidate promotion from final deployment selection.

title: LARK: Lean-Assisted Reasoning for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
authors: Zixi Zhang, Jiayi Nie, Haoran Wu et al.
abstract: Efficient GPU kernels are typically low-level and hardware-specific, and LLM agents can now generate them faster than experts can verify. Existing approaches rely on testing, which provides evidence but not a guarantee of correctness. We introduce LARK, an agentic framework that automatically and formally verifies GPU kernels against their PyTorch reference implementations. title: TrackMem: Tracking Evolving Beliefs in Long-Horizon Financial Dialogue
authors: Austin M. Y. Cheung, Harsh Vardhan Gupta, Go Nam Lui et al.
abstract: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, t

title: Beyond Prompt Injection: The Tool Update Gap in LLM Agent Security
authors: Shiyu Kan, Yue Qi, Yufei Han et al.
abstract: Large language model based agents increasingly rely on external tools to invoke services and interact with web resources. These tools can evolve through software updates, yet agentic frameworks may continue trusting them without re-verifying their safety after implementation changes. title: RECEIPT: Measuring and Repairing the Return Assumption of LLM Agents in Web Service Operations
authors: Boyang Yang, Ziyao Yang, Yu Zhang et al.
abstract: LLM agents operate Web infrastructure from the command line and rely on a return assumption, namely that each tool call returns within a bounded time and with its requested action finished. Many commands, however, ask a question before they act, and the agent's harness either closes the program's input or keeps it open as a terminal at which nobody types. title: AgenticMobility: An Open-Source Platform for Multi-AI-Agent Mobility Dynamics
authors: Jiaheng Xiao, Jiangtao Han, Jiachen Wang et al.
abstract: Understanding mobility dynamics and the effects of urban transportation management policies requires examining how individual travel decisions, traffic conditions, and policy interventions influence one another over time. We present AgenticMobility, an open-source experimental platform for studying how mobility AI agents and other AI agents interact, adapt through repeated experience, and collectively shape mobility outcomes. Persistent agents retain identities and relevant states across rounds,

title: NEIGHBOR: Aligning Service Behaviour and Evidence Use in an LLM Agent for Community Resident Services
authors: Zongyou Yang, Yinghan Hou, Xiaokun Yang
abstract: Residents who contact a community service desk about a repair or a service charge need answers they can act on, with facts that hold for their case and commitments the desk can keep. In tool-augmented LLM agents, such facts come from documents and records, and the conduct of a service answer is usually specified in a system prompt. title: LegoEnv: Self-Evolving Agentic Environments via Modular Recombination
authors: Zhuosong Jiang, Chengxu Wu, Junqi Liu et al.
abstract: LLM agents learn by interacting with environments, yet existing environments are designed for specific tasks and fail to generalize to new ones. Recent methods automate environment construction with LLMs. However, they generate each environment from scratch, neither reusing parts shared across environments nor carrying a fix from one environment to the rest. To address this, we propose a new paradigm of evolving environment atoms, which composes environments from reusable atoms (intent, rule, da

title: Evolving Memory, Learning to Meta-Control: Test-Time Adaptation for Experience-augmented LLM Agents
authors: Zeyuan Zhao, Yuanyuan Shi, Peng Yu et al.
abstract: Self-evolving agents accumulate experience from task streams, but existing frameworks typically rely on fixed pipelines to retrieve and utilize this experience, neglecting when and how to deploy it. We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience (OMCE), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. title: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks
authors: Zerui Chen, Qinggang Zhang, Qichuan Liu et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration p

title: Delivered, Not Used: Evaluating Agent Memory at Its Point of Use
authors: Changran Xu, Zeju Li, Qiang Xu
abstract: Task success, retrieval quality, and cost do not show whether an LLM agent used a delivered memory or what followed from that use. We introduce MemUse, which evaluates memory at its point of use in recorded trajectories: each memory delivery is compared with what the agent could already see and followed through the agent's later actions and their consequences. An agentic judge rates each delivered entry's relevance, accuracy, novelty, influence, and observed effect; programmatic checks enforce c

title: Just-in-Time Skill Retrieval via Long-Horizon State Tracking
authors: Xin Lin, Ziheng Wang, Zerui Chen et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external skill libraries to support complex task execution. However, determining which skills are needed remains challenging in long-horizon tasks. Existing methods typically select a fixed skill set before execution, implicitly assuming that a task's procedural requirements can be determined from its initial description. This assumption is restrictive for long-horizon interaction, where new requirements emerge from intermediate observations

title: CREDO: Evidence-Conditioned Credit Assignment for Temporal Reasoning Agents
authors: Yue Leng, Shengtao Wen, Xiang Chen et al.
abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) requires language model agents to retrieve evidence, select relevant facts, and perform multi-step temporal reasoning. However, the trajectory-level outcome signal in GRPO does not explicitly distinguish the quality of intermediate decisions: downstream failures can penalize useful evidence acquisition, while identical rewards in all-failed groups eliminate the relative outcome signal despite differences in intermediate progress. title: \textsc{ChatDify}: Automating End-to-End Dify Workflow Synthesis from Natural Language via Multi-Agent Collaboration
authors: Tao Fan, Guoqiang Ma
abstract: The proliferation of Large Language Models has catalyzed powerful application development platforms like Dify, which enable users to build sophisticated LLM-powered workflows through modular node orchestration. However, manually configuring these workflows requires deep platform expertise and remains time-consuming and error-prone, creating a significant barrier for non-expert users. To address this challenge, we propose \textsc{ChatDify}, a novel multi-agent framework that automates end-to-end

title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
authors: Haoyu Zhao, Zafeirios Fountas, Jun Wang
abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instruction

title: CONFIRM: Governing Scientific Reporting for Trustworthy Agentic Neuroimaging
authors: Yuxiang Wei, Lijing Zhu, Qizhen Lan et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can autonomously run neuroimaging analyses from research questions to reported findings. Existing agentic systems use tools to check that code runs and reported values match its output, but rely on LLM judgment to decide which results warrant scientific reporting. We show that LLM judges endorse site-confounded findings even when the confound is presented as evidence.
